claim: In humans, ageing is characterized by decreased brain signal variability.
source: In humans, ageing is characterized by decreased brain signal variability and increased behavioral variability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of ageing effects.

claim: In humans, ageing is characterized by increased behavioral variability.
source: In humans, ageing is characterized by decreased brain signal variability and increased behavioral variability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of ageing effects.

claim: Slow (<2 Hz) fluctuations of ongoing signals strongly modulated evoked responses.
source: Evoked responses were strongly modulated by slow (<2 Hz) fluctuations of the ongoing signals, which presented reduced power in the older participants.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slow (<2 Hz) fluctuations of ongoing signals presented reduced power in older participants.
source: Evoked responses were strongly modulated by slow (<2 Hz) fluctuations of the ongoing signals, which presented reduced power in the older participants.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated with spectral analyses.

claim: Variability of evoked responses was lower in older participants.
source: Although variability of the evoked responses was lower in the older participants, once we adjusted for the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations, evoked responses were equally variable in both groups.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical comparisons in the results.

claim: Once adjusted for the effect of ongoing signal fluctuations, evoked responses were equally variable in young and older adults.
source: Although variability of the evoked responses was lower in the older participants, once we adjusted for the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations, evoked responses were equally variable in both groups.
evidence: This is a key finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated through statistical analyses after adjustment.

claim: The modulation of evoked responses caused by ongoing signal fluctuations had no impact on reaction time.
source: Moreover, the modulation of the evoked responses caused by the ongoing signal fluctuations had no impact on reaction time, thereby explaining why although ongoing brain signal variability is decreased in older individuals, behavioral variability is not.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analyses in the results section.

claim: Adjusting for the effect of the ongoing signal was critical to unmask the link between neural responses and behavior.
source: Finally, we showed that adjusting for the effect of the ongoing signal was critical to unmask the link between neural responses and behavior as well as the link between task-related evoked EEG and pupil responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through correlation analyses before and after adjustment.

claim: Adjusting for the effect of the ongoing signal was critical to unmask the link between task-related evoked EEG and pupil responses.
source: Finally, we showed that adjusting for the effect of the ongoing signal was critical to unmask the link between neural responses and behavior as well as the link between task-related evoked EEG and pupil responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through correlation analyses.

claim: Within-subject brain signal variability has been shown to change with ageing and is a robust marker of age.
source: Within-subject brain signal variability has been shown to change with ageing and is a robust marker of age (Grady and Garrett, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The temporal standard deviation of the BOLD signal is markedly decreased in older adults.
source: The temporal standard deviation of the BOLD signal and of the amplitude envelop of EEG frequency bands measured in the ongoing signal are markedly decreased in older adults (Garrett et al., 2015; Grady and Garrett, 2018; Kumral et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The temporal standard deviation of the amplitude envelope of EEG frequency bands measured in the ongoing signal is markedly decreased in older adults.
source: The temporal standard deviation of the BOLD signal and of the amplitude envelop of EEG frequency bands measured in the ongoing signal are markedly decreased in older adults (Garrett et al., 2015; Grady and Garrett, 2018; Kumral et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The localization of changes in BOLD and EEG variability does not coincide, suggesting that BOLD and EEG variability capture different aspects of brain function.
source: Yet, the localization of these changes does not coincide suggesting that BOLD and EEG variability capture different aspects of brain function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings from different studies.

claim: Age differences in BOLD SD might be explained by changes in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular factors that affect the link between neuronal activity and changes in blood flow.
source: In fact, age differences in BOLD SD might be explained by changes in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular factors that affect the link between neuronal activity and changes in blood flow (Tsvetanov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BOLD MSSD is more often increased rather than decreased in older adults.
source: Moreover, BOLD MSSD, a measure of how much the BOLD signal changes across successive observations, is more often increased rather than decreased in older adults (Boylan et al., 2021; Nomi et al., 2017; Samanez-Larkin et al., 2010), highlighting the fact that age-related changes in signal dynamics can result in more or less 'signal variability' depending on the used metric.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Older adults present EEG signals with flatter spectra, potentially reflecting increased neuronal noise.
source: Older adults present EEG signals with flatter spectra, i.e., more similar to white noise, potentially reflecting increased neuronal noise (Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and includes speculation about the interpretation.

claim: Older people present increased behavioral variability measured as less consistent reaction time across trials.
source: Higher brain noise is also consistent with the fact that older people present increased behavioral variability measured as less consistent reaction time across trials (Grady and Garrett, 2018; MacDonald et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing activity modulates task-related evoked responses that in turn affect task performance.
source: Not surprisingly, ongoing activity modulates task-related evoked responses that in turn affect task performance (Becker et al., 2011; Fox et al., 2007; Mayhew et al., 2013; Ribeiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fluctuations in pre-stimulus alpha power affect the amplitude of brain sensory responses, perception and reaction time.
source: For example, fluctuations in pre-stimulus alpha power affect the amplitude of brain sensory responses, perception and reaction time (Lou et al., 2014; Thut et al., 2006; van Dijk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Older people display low-frequency (<12 Hz) brain signal fluctuations with reduced amplitude.
source: Older people display low-frequency (<12 Hz) brain signal fluctuations with reduced amplitude (Kumral et al., 2020), however, previous studies of the effect of ageing on the variability of task evoked responses have yielded contradictory results, revealing increased or decreased trial-by-trial consistency depending on stimulus or task characteristics (Sander et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2020; Wiegand and Sander, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies of the effect of ageing on the variability of task evoked responses have yielded contradictory results, revealing increased or decreased trial-by-trial consistency depending on stimulus or task characteristics.
source: Older people display low-frequency (<12 Hz) brain signal fluctuations with reduced amplitude (Kumral et al., 2020), however, previous studies of the effect of ageing on the variability of task evoked responses have yielded contradictory results, revealing increased or decreased trial-by-trial consistency depending on stimulus or task characteristics (Sander et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2020; Wiegand and Sander, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study included 36 young adults (mean age ± SD = 23±3 years).
source: Thirty-six young adults (mean age ± SD = 23±3 years; 29 women; 3 left-handed) and thirty-nine older adults (mean age ± SD = 60±5 years; 31 women; 3 left-handed) were included in this study.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: The study included 39 older adults (mean age ± SD = 60±5 years).
source: Thirty-six young adults (mean age ± SD = 23±3 years; 29 women; 3 left-handed) and thirty-nine older adults (mean age ± SD = 60±5 years; 31 women; 3 left-handed) were included in this study.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Reaction time variability was significantly higher in the older group.
source: Nevertheless, reaction time variability (within-subject across trials SD) was significantly higher in the older group [t(73)=–2.53, p= 0.013].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The older participants were on average slower responding to the go stimulus, but this difference was not statistically significant.
source: The older participants were on average slower responding to the go stimulus; however, this difference was not statistically significant [t(73)=–1.84, p= 0.070].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Reaction time coefficient of variation was not significantly different across groups.
source: Reaction time coefficient of variation was not significantly different across groups [t(73)=–1.57, p= 0.120].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The number of errors of commission was not significantly different across groups.
source: The number of errors of commission was not significantly different across groups (U=627, p=0.400; median of one error of commission across participants in each group, with 64% and 66% of young and older participants responding at least once to the no-go stimulus).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Misses occurred more often in the older group.
source: In contrast, misses and responses to the cue occurred more often in the older group. Mann-Whitney tests revealed a significant effect of group for the number of misses (U=552, p=0.050, 22% of young participants presented at least one missed trial in comparison with 38% of older participants)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Responses to the cue occurred more often in the older group.
source: and responses to the cue (U=538, p=0.022, 14% of young participants incorrectly responded to the cue stimuli at least once in comparison with 36% of older participants).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Trial-by-trial variability in the CNV amplitude was decreased in the older group.
source: Trial-by-trial variability in the CNV amplitude (CNV variability) was decreased in the older group (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2 showing the data.

claim: The CNV showed strongest amplitude in the frontocentral electrode FCz.
source: During the preparatory period between the cue and the target, a frontocentral negative potential (the CNV) could be observed in the EEG of both groups of participants with strongest amplitude in the frontocentral electrode FCz (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The amplitude of the CNV was on average stronger (more negative) in the older group.
source: Although the amplitude of this evoked response was on average stronger (more negative) in the older group, trial-by-trial variability (across trials standard deviation) was reduced in the older group (Figure 2B and D; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1f for single subject examples of trial-by-trial CNV variability).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: CNV amplitude presented strongest group difference in left central electrodes.
source: CNV amplitude presented strongest group difference in left central electrodes, while CNV variability presented strongest group difference in parieto-occipital electrodes.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the topographic distributions of group differences.

claim: CNV variability presented strongest group difference in parieto-occipital electrodes.
source: CNV amplitude presented strongest group difference in left central electrodes, while CNV variability presented strongest group difference in parieto-occipital electrodes.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the topographic distributions of group differences.

claim: Trial-by-trial CNV amplitude fluctuations were associated with reaction time fluctuations.
source: Trial-by-trial CNV amplitude fluctuations were associated with reaction time fluctuations (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3 showing correlation analyses.

claim: Within-subject correlation analyses revealed a significant relationship between CNV amplitude and reaction time.
source: Within-subject correlation analyses revealed a significant relationship between CNV amplitude and reaction time.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by statistical analyses.

claim: The correlation values between CNV amplitude and reaction time were significantly different from zero in a left frontocentral cluster of electrodes.
source: The correlation values were significantly different from zero in a left frontocentral cluster of electrodes (one-sample t-tests including all participants; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The CNV is comprised of different components including a motor-related late component.
source: The CNV is comprised of different components including a motor-related late component (Nagai et al., 2004; van Boxtel and Böcker, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The association between CNV amplitude and reaction time results from preparatory motor activity happening during that period.
source: This result suggests that the association between CNV amplitude and reaction time results from preparatory motor activity happening during that period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the topographic distribution of the correlation.

claim: Older individuals presented reduced trial-by-trial variability in cue-locked pupil dilation responses.
source: Older individuals presented reduced trial-by-trial variability in cue-locked pupil dilation (PD) responses (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The warning cue elicited a pupil dilation response that peaked around 3 s after cue-onset.
source: The warning cue elicited a pupil dilation response that peaked around 3 s after cue-onset (as reported before in Ribeiro and Castelo-Branco, 2019a; replotted in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 4A, and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PD response amplitude was not significantly different across groups.
source: PD response amplitude was not significantly different across groups [t(71)=–1.82, p=0.073].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the pupil data analysis.

claim: The variability of PD response amplitude was significantly reduced in the older group.
source: The variability of PD response amplitude was, however, significantly reduced in the older group [t(71)=6.05, p<0.001; Figure 4B; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for single subject examples of trial-by-trial variability in evoked responses].
evidence: This is a statistical finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Preparatory pupil dilation responses did not correlate with reaction time.
source: Preparatory pupil dilation responses did not correlate with reaction time. Within-subject correlation coefficients were not significantly different across groups [t(71)=1.10, p=0.276] or significantly different from zero [one-sample t-test including all participants, t(72) = 0.670, p=0.505].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analyses.

claim: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented power spectral density data that are less steep.
source: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented power spectral density (PSD) data that are less steep, with reduced offset (reduced amplitude at low frequencies), reduced alpha power and increased beta power (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented reduced offset (reduced amplitude at low frequencies).
source: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented power spectral density (PSD) data that are less steep, with reduced offset (reduced amplitude at low frequencies), reduced alpha power and increased beta power (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented reduced alpha power.
source: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented power spectral density (PSD) data that are less steep, with reduced offset (reduced amplitude at low frequencies), reduced alpha power and increased beta power (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented increased beta power.
source: The ongoing EEG signal of older adults presented power spectral density (PSD) data that are less steep, with reduced offset (reduced amplitude at low frequencies), reduced alpha power and increased beta power (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both the spectral exponent and offset were significantly reduced in the older group.
source: Both were significantly reduced in the older group (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Occipital alpha power was reduced in older individuals mainly in occipital channels.
source: Occipital alpha power was reduced in older individuals mainly in occipital channels.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the spectral analysis results.

claim: Beta power in frontal and central EEG channels was increased in the older group.
source: In contrast, beta power in frontal and central EEG channels was increased in the older group.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the spectral analysis results.

claim: The PSDs of ongoing pupil signals of older individuals presented reduced exponent and offset.
source: The PSDs of ongoing pupil signals of older individuals presented reduced exponent and offset (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The spectra of the ongoing pupillary signal followed a 1/f distribution, with power decreasing with increasing frequency.
source: The spectra of the ongoing pupillary signal followed a 1 /f distribution, with power decreasing with increasing frequency (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The aperiodic parameters of the pupil signal were significantly decreased in the older group.
source: The aperiodic parameters were significantly decreased in the older group [exponent: t(70) = 7.48, p<0.001; offset: t(70) = 4.17, p<0.001], that is the older group presented a flatter pupil spectrum with lower amplitude at the low frequencies.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the pupil spectral analysis.

claim: No obvious peaks were detected in the pupil spectra.
source: No obvious peaks were detected in the pupil spectra.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the pupil spectral analysis results.

claim: Participants with higher spectral offset and exponent presented higher CNV variability.
source: Participants with higher spectral offset and exponent presented higher CNV and PD variability (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7 with correlation analyses.

claim: Participants with higher spectral offset and exponent presented higher PD variability.
source: Participants with higher spectral offset and exponent presented higher CNV and PD variability (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7 with correlation analyses.

claim: Alpha power presented a positive association with CNV variability only in the young group and in posterior EEG channels.
source: Alpha power presented a positive association with CNV variability only in the young group and in posterior EEG channels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Beta power was not associated with CNV variability.
source: Beta power was not associated with CNV variability.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: The correlation between variability in the amplitude of the evoked responses and the amplitude of the power spectra was particularly strong in the lower frequencies.
source: We found that the correlation between variability in the amplitude of the evoked responses and the amplitude of the power spectra was particularly strong in the lower frequencies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the total spectral power, the correlation between PD variability and spectral power was highest around 0.44 Hz.
source: In the total spectral power, the correlation between PD variability and spectral power was highest around 0.44 Hz and decreased for lower frequencies.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: In the EEG analyses, correlation between CNV variability and spectral power was highest at 1 Hz, the lowest frequency analysed.
source: In the EEG analyses, correlation was highest at 1 Hz, the lowest frequency analysed.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: The group differences in CNV variability were markedly reduced once the effect of the spectral exponent, offset or slow spectral power were regressed out.
source: The group differences in CNV and PD variability were markedly reduced once the effect of the spectral exponent, offset or slow spectral power were regressed out (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8 with statistical analyses.

claim: The group differences in PD variability were markedly reduced once the effect of the spectral exponent, offset or slow spectral power were regressed out.
source: The group differences in CNV and PD variability were markedly reduced once the effect of the spectral exponent, offset or slow spectral power were regressed out (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8 with statistical analyses.

claim: After adjusting for the confounds, the CNV variability was no longer significantly different across groups.
source: In fact, after adjusting for the confounds, the CNV variability was no longer significantly different across groups [adjusting for exponent t(72) = 0.661, p=0.511; adjusting for offset t(72) = 0.243, p=0.809; adjusting for slow spectral power t(72) = 0.979, p=0.331; Figure 8].
evidence: This is a statistical finding shown in Figure 8.

claim: The group difference in the PD variability was completely explained by the power of slow fluctuations observed in the ongoing pupillary signal.
source: The group difference in the PD variability was also completely explained by the power of slow fluctuations observed in the ongoing pupillary signal [t-test group comparison no longer significant: t(71) = 1.54, p=0.129; Figure 8].
evidence: This is a statistical finding shown in Figure 8.

claim: The evoked responses showed a dependence on the phase of the ongoing fluctuations in line with what would be expected if the measured evoked responses were the summation of an evoked response with an ongoing fluctuating signal.
source: The evoked responses showed a dependence on the phase of the ongoing fluctuations in line with what would be expected if the measured evoked responses were the summation of an evoked response with an ongoing fluctuating signal (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9.

claim: The CNV amplitude depended on time-on-task.
source: The EEG GLM revealed that the CNV amplitude depended on time-on-task [it became less negative with time-on-task; t(73) = 2.84, p=0.006; Figure 9A]
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The CNV amplitude depended on the phase of the ongoing fluctuations at cue-onset captured by the cosine and sine functions.
source: and on the phase of the ongoing fluctuations at cue-onset captured by the cosine [t(73)=–36.3, p<0.001] and the sine [t(73)=–81.7, p<0.001] functions (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The CNV amplitude was independent of run and pre-stimulus alpha power.
source: It was independent of run [t(73)=0.035, p=0.973] and pre-stimulus alpha power [t(73)=–0.530, p=0.598].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis.

claim: Time-on-task had a stronger effect on the evoked responses of the young group in comparison with the older group.
source: Time-on-task had a stronger effect on the evoked responses of the young group in comparison with the older group [independent samples t-test: t(72) = 3.74, p<0.001].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis.

claim: The only predictors that significantly contributed towards trial-by-trial PD variability were the cosine and the sine of the pre-stimulus phase.
source: The pupil GLM revealed that the only predictors that significantly contributed towards trial-by-trial PD variability were the cosine and the sine of the pre-stimulus phase [one-sample t-test testing estimated coefficients against zero - cosine: t(71) = –38.2, p<0.001; sine: t(71) = –51.3, p<0.001].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis.

claim: After regressing out the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations from the amplitude of the evoked responses, these were associated with reaction time at least as strongly as without the adjustment.
source: After regressing out the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations from the amplitude of the evoked responses, these were associated with reaction time at least as strongly as without the adjustment.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: Regressing out the effect of ongoing signal fluctuations was crucial to detect the link between PD evoked responses and reaction time.
source: For the pupil responses, we found that regressing out the effect of ongoing signal fluctuations was crucial to detect the link between PD evoked responses and reaction time, that is the PD amplitude residuals correlated with reaction time [Figure 11C; one-sample t-test: t(72) = –4.77, p<0.001].
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 11C with statistical analyses.

claim: The correlation coefficients between PD amplitude residuals and reaction time with the adjustment for the phase of the ongoing signal were significantly different from the coefficients without the adjustment.
source: Notably, the correlation coefficients with the adjustment for the phase of the ongoing signal were significantly different from the coefficients without the adjustment [paired t-test comparing with and without adjustment: t(72) = –5.08, p<0.001].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: After regressing out the effect of the ongoing signal's phase at cue-onset, the variability of the evoked responses was still significantly reduced in the older group.
source: It is important to note that after regressing out the effect of the ongoing signal's phase at cue-onset, the variability of the evoked responses was still significantly reduced in the older group (Figure 11—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the baseline (pre-stimulus) values are not enough to completely predict the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations on the evoked responses in line with the idea that these slow signal fluctuations are aperiodic and therefore not completely predictable (Shimaoka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1 with a citation.

claim: The single trial measurements of the CNV and pupil responses were significantly correlated.
source: In within-subject correlation analyses, we found that the single trial measurements of the CNV and pupil responses were significantly correlated with stronger correlation coefficients observed in posterior channels (Figure 12A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The correlation coefficients between CNV and pupil responses were stronger when the pupil response was measured 500ms after the CNV measurements.
source: The correlation coefficients were stronger when the pupil response was measured 500ms after the CNV measurements.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: The correlations between CNV and pupil responses were stronger after adjusting for the ongoing slow signal fluctuations.
source: Just like for the correlations with task performance, these correlations were stronger after adjusting for the ongoing slow signal fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the correlation analysis results.

claim: The reaction time variance explained by the model including CNV and pupil residuals was significantly higher than the variance explained by the model including only the pupil dilation residuals or the model including only the CNV residuals.
source: The reaction time variance explained by the model including CNV and pupil residuals was significantly higher than the variance explained by the model including only the pupil dilation residuals or the model including only the CNV residuals [Figure 12C; R2 across participants mean ± SD: pupil only model young group = 2% ± 3%; pupil only model older group = 2% ± 3%; CNV only model young group (average across channels)=2% ± 2%; CNV only model older group (average across channels)=4% ± 4%; pupil +CNV model young group (average across channels)=4% ± 3%; pupil +CNV model older group (average across channels)=7% ± 4 %].
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 12C with statistical analyses.

claim: The pupil dilation response and the CNV contribute independently towards behavior variability.
source: These findings suggest that the pupil dilation response and the CNV contribute independently towards behavior variability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multiple regression analysis results.

claim: At baseline (before cue onset), the descending phase of the slow signal fluctuations in the EEG in left temporal channels was associated with faster responses.
source: In summary, at baseline (before cue onset), the descending phase of the slow signal fluctuations in the EEG in left temporal channels and bigger pupils were associated with faster responses.
evidence: This is stated in the text summarizing the analysis results.

claim: At baseline (before cue onset), bigger pupils were associated with faster responses.
source: In summary, at baseline (before cue onset), the descending phase of the slow signal fluctuations in the EEG in left temporal channels and bigger pupils were associated with faster responses.
evidence: This is stated in the text summarizing the analysis results.

claim: Task-related brain evoked responses occur on top of ongoing signal fluctuations that markedly affect their amplitude on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: Task-related brain evoked responses occur on top of ongoing signal fluctuations that markedly affect their amplitude on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: As a consequence of older people showing reduced amplitude in the ongoing slow signal fluctuations measured in the EEG and pupil signals, trial-by-trial variability in their evoked responses is also decreased.
source: Our results revealed that as a consequence of older people showing reduced amplitude in the ongoing slow signal fluctuations measured in the EEG and pupil signals, trial-by-trial variability in their evoked responses is also decreased.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Once the difference in ongoing signal dynamics was adjusted for, the evoked responses were equally variable in young and older adults.
source: Once the difference in ongoing signal dynamics was adjusted for, the evoked responses were equally variable in young and older adults.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Although ongoing signal fluctuations strongly affected the amplitude of the evoked responses, these amplitude modulations did not appear to have behavioral consequences.
source: In fact, although ongoing signal fluctuations strongly affected the amplitude of the evoked responses, these amplitude modulations did not appear to have behavioral consequences.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The effect of the ongoing fluctuations on the evoked responses is purely additive and simply reflects the fluctuating baseline.
source: The other possibility assumes that the effect of the ongoing fluctuations on the evoked responses is purely additive and simply reflects the fluctuating baseline and is therefore not relevant for the type of task studied. This second hypothesis is supported by previous fMRI studies in humans (Fox et al., 2006; Schölvinck et al., 2012) as well as studies of neuronal responses measured in the sensory cortices of mice and cats (Schölvinck et al., 2015; Shimaoka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The variance of the evoked responses explained by the models tested increased substantially by including the ongoing signal phase at cue-onset in comparison with including only the signal amplitude.
source: Indeed, similar baseline amplitude levels at different signal phases (with amplitude increasing or amplitude decreasing) have different effects on the amplitude of the evoked responses (see Figure 9) and the variance of the evoked responses explained by the models tested increased substantially by including the ongoing signal phase [r • sin(θ)] at cue-onset in comparison with including only the signal amplitude (as captured by the cosine function).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the GLM analysis results.

claim: When we adjusted for the effect of the ongoing fluctuations on the evoked response's amplitude, the correlation between the evoked response and reaction time was at least as strong as without this adjustment.
source: Importantly, when we adjusted for the effect of the ongoing fluctuations on the evoked response's amplitude, the correlation between the evoked response and reaction time was at least as strong as without this adjustment, suggesting that the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations on the evoked responses has no impact on behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: In both the pupil and EEG signals adjusting for ongoing signal fluctuations unmasked a relationship between the evoked responses amplitude and reaction time that, without the adjustment, was not detectable in the pupil and was evident only in a restricted number of channels in the EEG.
source: Interestingly, in both the pupil and EEG signals adjusting for ongoing signal fluctuations unmasked a relationship between the evoked responses amplitude and reaction time that, without the adjustment, was not detectable in the pupil and was evident only in a restricted number of channels in the EEG.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The additional variability imposed on the evoked responses by the ongoing signal can mask brain-behavior associations.
source: This observation suggests that the additional variability imposed on the evoked responses by the ongoing signal can mask brain-behavior associations and therefore should be attended to and adjusted for.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis results.

claim: The pupillogram, acquired under conditions of constant luminance, is associated with fluctuations in arousal and reflects activity in the ascending brainstem neuromodulatory systems.
source: The EEG allows the non-invasive measurement of cortical electrical activity with high temporal resolution, while the pupillogram, acquired under conditions of constant luminance, is associated with fluctuations in arousal and reflects activity in the ascending brainstem neuromodulatory systems (de Gee et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity modulation in subcortical arousal nuclei (reflected in changes in pupil size) correlates with the EEG signal.
source: Although, activity modulation in subcortical arousal nuclei (reflected in changes in pupil size) correlates with the EEG signal (e.g. Hong et al., 2014; Podvalny et al., 2021), these two signals capture distinct aspects of brain function, both important and complementary for our understanding of the ageing brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CNV has been previously shown to correlate with reaction time on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: The CNV has been previously shown to correlate with reaction time on a trial-by-trial basis (Boehm et al., 2014), suggesting that trial-by-trial amplitude fluctuations in the CNV are associated with behavioral variability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The CNV preparatory potential originates from a set of brain areas, including the supplementary motor area (SMA), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the thalamus.
source: The CNV preparatory potential originates not from an unitary neural mechanism but from a set of brain areas, including the supplementary motor area (SMA), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the thalamus (Nagai et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A correlation between the CNV and the pupil dilation response had already been suggested before on between-subjects correlation analysis.
source: A correlation between the CNV and the pupil dilation response had already been suggested before on between-subjects correlation analysis (Hepsomali et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The pupil response is slow and lags the associated cortical events by hundreds of milliseconds.
source: We found that the correlation was stronger when comparing the CNV amplitude with the pupil dilation measured with a 500 ms delay in line with the idea that the pupil response is slow and lags the associated cortical events by hundreds of milliseconds (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Activity in the ACC is observed during preparatory periods associated with the CNV potential.
source: Activity in the ACC is observed during preparatory periods associated with the CNV potential (Nagai et al., 2004) and it is associated with pupil dilation events (Joshi et al., 2016; Joshi and Gold, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activity in the ACC is associated with pupil dilation events.
source: Activity in the ACC is observed during preparatory periods associated with the CNV potential (Nagai et al., 2004) and it is associated with pupil dilation events (Joshi et al., 2016; Joshi and Gold, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ageing affects the dynamics of the ongoing EEG signal (reflecting cortical activity) and the ongoing pupillary signal (reflecting activity in brainstem neuromodulatory systems).
source: Our analyses showed that ageing affects the dynamics of the ongoing EEG signal (reflecting cortical activity) and the ongoing pupillary signal (reflecting activity in brainstem neuromodulatory systems).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: In both EEG and pupil signals, older people presented flatter spectra with reduced power in the slower aperiodic fluctuations.
source: In both signals, older people presented flatter spectra with reduced power in the slower aperiodic fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The flattening of brain signal spectra with ageing has been described before in EEG and ECoG data.
source: This flattening of brain signal spectra with ageing has been described before in EEG and ECoG data (Voytek et al., 2015; Waschke et al., 2017), is also evident in MEG data (Vlahou et al., 2014), and is here reported in the pupil signal suggesting an age-related decrease in the amplitude of the slow fluctuations in cortical and subcortical networks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In MEG data, the power of slow fluctuations decreases linearly with ageing.
source: In line with our findings, Vlahou et al., 2014 showed that, in MEG data, the power of slow fluctuations decreases linearly with ageing (Vlahou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sequential activation and de-activation of resting-state networks is observed in the ongoing EEG data both during rest and task performance.
source: Sequential activation and de-activation of resting-state networks is observed in the ongoing EEG data both during rest and task performance (Abreu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ageing is characterized by a significant decrease in the strength of long-range structural connections.
source: Ageing is characterized by a significant decrease in the strength of long-range structural connections (Westlye et al., 2010) as well as a decrease in the functional connectivity (correlated BOLD activation patterns) within large-scale brain systems, like the default mode network (Sala-Llonch et al., 2015), consistent with the idea that simultaneous activation of distant brain areas supported by long-range structural connectivity is impaired in older individuals (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ageing is characterized by a decrease in the functional connectivity within large-scale brain systems, like the default mode network.
source: Ageing is characterized by a significant decrease in the strength of long-range structural connections (Westlye et al., 2010) as well as a decrease in the functional connectivity (correlated BOLD activation patterns) within large-scale brain systems, like the default mode network (Sala-Llonch et al., 2015), consistent with the idea that simultaneous activation of distant brain areas supported by long-range structural connectivity is impaired in older individuals (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduced amplitude of slow EEG fluctuations might be related to impaired recruitment of large-scale brain systems.
source: Reduced amplitude of slow EEG fluctuations might therefore be related to impaired recruitment of large-scale brain systems.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and previous literature.

claim: The age-related increase in reaction time variability depends on the task used to measure it.
source: The age-related increase in reaction time variability depends on the task used to measure it (Dykiert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The age difference in reaction time variability is smaller in simple RT tasks than in choice tasks.
source: For example, the age difference in reaction time variability is smaller in simple RT tasks than in choice tasks and is smaller in tasks using longer preparatory intervals as the ones used in our task (Dykiert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The age difference in reaction time variability is smaller in tasks using longer preparatory intervals.
source: For example, the age difference in reaction time variability is smaller in simple RT tasks than in choice tasks and is smaller in tasks using longer preparatory intervals as the ones used in our task (Dykiert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The study shows that the amplitude of the preparatory evoked potential, the CNV, and the preparatory pupil dilation responses show comparable trial-by-trial variability in young and older adults once the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations is considered.
source: The current study shows that the amplitude of the preparatory evoked potential, the CNV, and the preparatory pupil dilation responses show comparable trial-by-trial variability in young and older adults once the effect of the ongoing signal fluctuations is considered.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as a summary of the main finding.

claim: This finding suggests a dissociation between ongoing brain activity, which presents reduced variability in older adults, and task-related responses, which do not.
source: This finding suggests a dissociation between ongoing brain activity, which presents reduced variability in older adults, and task-related responses, which do not.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the main findings.

claim: This dissociation might explain why although ongoing brain activity is less variable in older adults, behavior variability increases with ageing.
source: This dissociation might explain why although ongoing brain activity is less variable in older adults, behavior variability increases with ageing.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.
